title: The Union Executive
tagline: President, Vice-President, Prime Minister and Council of Ministers: how executive power is held and answerable.

overview.intro: The Union Executive is where the Constitution reconciles two ideas that pull in opposite directions: a head of State elected indirectly and vested with the whole executive power of the Union, and a Prime Minister who in practice directs the government and answers to the Lok Sabha. This chapter separates the two clearly — the President’s election, tenure and impeachment, the President’s powers article by article, the Vice-President’s dual role, and then the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers with their collective and individual responsibility. The recurring examination trap is that almost every executive act is done by the President on the advice of the Council of Ministers, and the answer that scores names both.

facts.label: President
facts.value: Elected indirectly by an Electoral College of elected MPs and elected MLAs; term five years.

facts.label: Impeachment
facts.value: Charge by one House with a two-thirds majority of its total membership, trial by the other, on the charge of violating the Constitution.

facts.label: Vice-President
facts.value: Elected by members of both Houses and ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha; term five years.

facts.label: Council of Ministers
facts.value: Appointed by the President on the Prime Minister’s advice; collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.

learningOutcomes: Explain the composition of the Electoral College and why the election is indirect.
Describe the President’s powers under the executive, legislative, financial, judicial, discretionary and emergency heads.
State the qualifications, term and removal procedure of the President and the Vice-President.
Explain how the Prime Minister is appointed and how the Council of Ministers is collectively and individually responsible.
Distinguish the Council of Ministers from the Cabinet and give two functions of each that the question asks for.

learn.title: Election, tenure and impeachment of the President

blocks.text: The President is elected by an Electoral College consisting of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies, including the legislatures of Delhi and Puducherry. Nominated members are excluded, which is the point examiners test most often, and so are the members of Union Territory legislatures that have no Assembly of their own. The election uses proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote and secret ballots, a system that makes the value of an MP’s vote different from the value of an MLA’s so that parity between the Houses and between the States is preserved. The term is five years, and the President remains in office until a successor takes charge. Removal is by impeachment for violation of the Constitution: one House passes the charge by a majority of not less than two thirds of its total membership, the other House investigates, and a similar majority there convicts, after which the President ceases to hold office. Fourteen days’ notice must precede the charge.

items: Electoral College: elected MPs plus elected MLAs of the States and of the legislatures of Delhi and Puducherry.
Excluded from voting: nominated members of Parliament, nominated members of State Assemblies, members of legislatures without Assembly status and members of Councils of States.
Value of an MLA’s vote: total value of the State’s population divided by a thousand, divided by the number of elected MLAs, plus one.
Term of office is five years, but the President may continue until a successor is elected and takes charge.
Impeachment lies only for violation of the Constitution and requires two thirds of the total membership of each House in turn.

A system in which a voter orders candidates by preference and a candidate is elected once a quota of first and transferred preferences is reached.

learn.title: The President’s powers, head by head

blocks.text: Presidential powers are conventionally listed under six heads, and a structured answer names the head first and gives instances under it. Executive power covers all executive action in the name of the President and the appointment of Governors, Prime Ministers, judges, the Attorney-General, the Comptroller and Auditor-General and the Election Commission. Legislative power includes summoning and proroguing Parliament, addressing it at its first session after a general election, dissolving the Lok Sabha, and promulgating an ordinance when Parliament is not in session. Financial power runs through the annual financial statement, the consent needed for money bills and the contingency fund. Judicial power covers appointments, pardons, reprieves, respites and remissions, and references to the Supreme Court under Article 143. Discretionary power is narrow: choosing a Prime Minister when no party has a clear majority and sending a message back to Parliament in certain cases. Emergency power under Article 352, 356 and 360 is treated separately because of its scope.

items: Executive: appoints the Prime Minister and, on that advice, the Council of Ministers, the Governors, judges and the constitutional authorities.
Legislative: summons, prorogues and dissolves Parliament; addresses the first session after a general election; promulgates ordinances under Article 123.
Financial: the annual financial statement is laid before Parliament in the President’s name; no money may be drawn from the Consolidated Fund except under an appropriation by law.
Judicial: pardons, reprieves, respites and remissions of sentence, and pardon is a power that only the President or a Governor holds.
Discretionary: appoints the leader who commands the majority, and may send a message to the Houses for reconsideration of a bill, which the Houses may override.
Emergency: Proclamation of Emergency under Article 352, President’s Rule under Article 356 and Financial Emergency under Article 360, each with its own limits.

items.note: With Parliament out of session the President promulgates an ordinance under Article 123; it has the force of an Act but must be laid before Parliament and lapses six weeks after reassembly unless approved.
The President’s pardon power under Article 72 is independent of the government of the day in form, though in practice exercised on the advice of the Council of Ministers.

learn.title: The Vice-President: two offices in one person

blocks.text: The Vice-President is elected by members of both Houses of Parliament, including nominated members, by proportional representation by means of a single transferable vote in a secret ballot — the difference from the Presidential election, where nominated members are excluded, is a classic one-mark trap. The term is five years, and removal follows a procedure of its own: a resolution for removal must be passed by the Council of States by a majority of all its members and agreed to by the Lok Sabha by a majority of its total membership, so removal is harder than ordinary business. The Vice-President holds two offices: Vice-President of India, the constitutional successor to the President, and ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, in which capacity the Vice-President is not a member of the House but presides over it and has a casting vote. Because the two roles are different, a Vice-President who is re-elected as Chairman may be succeeded in the Vice-Presidency by a new election.

items: Election: by members of both Houses, nominated members included, by single transferable vote and secret ballot.
Term: five years; qualification: citizen of India, 35 years of age and qualified to be a member of the Rajya Sabha.
Removal: by a resolution of the Council of States passed by all its members and agreed to by the Lok Sabha by a majority of its total membership.
As Chairman the Vice-President may vote in the Council of States only to break an equality, except on a matter requiring a majority of the total membership.
If the office of President falls vacant, the Vice-President acts as President until a new President is elected.

items.text: Who signs the warrant of removal
items.note: A resolution to remove the Vice-President must first be passed by the Rajya Sabha and only then be taken up by the Lok Sabha, which is the reverse of the ordinary Bill route.
When the Council of States divides equally on a bill, the Chairman may exercise the casting vote to resolve the equality.

learn.title: The Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers

blocks.text: The Prime Minister is appointed by the President as the person most likely to command the confidence of the Lok Sabha, which in practice means the leader of the majority party after a general election. The President then appoints the other ministers on the Prime Minister’s advice, and they hold office during the pleasure of the President — a pleasure that, since the Supreme Court’s judgment in the S.K. Antony case, cannot be exercised independently of the Prime Minister’s advice. Ministers are drawn from the two Houses, and a person who is not a member of either may be appointed but must secure a seat in one of them within six months. The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha: it stands or falls together, and the loss of a confidence motion requires the whole Council to resign. Individual responsibility means that each minister is answerable for the portfolio he or she holds and may be asked to resign for a failure in that department. The Council includes Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State with independent charge and Ministers of State attached to a Cabinet Minister; the Cabinet is the inner core that takes the major decisions and meets in a smaller room with a fixed agenda.

items: Appointment: the Prime Minister is appointed by the President; other ministers are appointed by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister.
Collective responsibility: Article 75(3) makes the Council responsible to the Lok Sabha, so the fall of the government on a confidence motion requires the whole Council to resign.
Individual responsibility: each minister answers for his or her own portfolio and may be removed for failure within it.
A minister must be a member of either House within six months of appointment, failing which the ministership lapses.
The Cabinet: the senior-most ministers who take the major policy decisions, meet on a fixed agenda, and whose decisions bind all other ministers under the doctrine of collective responsibility.
Shadow Cabinet: the Opposition’s team of spokespeople mirroring the Cabinet, a term asked for in one-mark questions but not a part of the Constitution.

learn.title: Answering questions on the Union Executive

blocks.text: Executive questions are the ones where candidates lose marks by being vague. Three habits prevent that. First, always separate what the President does from who decides it: write the President’s name in the sentence and add the phrase on the advice of the Council of Ministers where the Constitution requires it, because a full-mark answer on the executive shows that the President is the constitutional head rather than the decision-maker. Second, use the headings the question asks for — a question asking for executive, legislative and judicial powers wants three paragraphs, not six undifferentiated lines. Third, attach an article where the syllabus expects one: Articles 52 and 53 for the President’s office, 54 and 55 for the election, 61 for impeachment, 64 for the Vice-President as Chairman, 74 for the Council of Ministers and 75 for their appointment and responsibility. Finish every long answer with a line on the practical significance — the emergency provisions, the ordinance power or the confidence requirement — because that is what converts a description into an explanation.

items: Name the President as the constitutional head and add the advice phrase wherever the Constitution requires it.
Give the article with the feature: 54 election, 61 impeachment, 64 Vice-President as Chairman, 74 aid and advice, 75(3) responsibility.
Distinguish Council of Ministers from Cabinet by size, frequency of meeting and scope of decisions.
Close a ten-mark answer with the significance of the provision for the working of democracy.

items.note: Open with executive, legislative and financial powers in order, give one instance for each, then judicial and discretionary, then a closing line on emergency provisions.

items.text: A distinguish between Council and Cabinet
items.note: Answer in four rows: size, meetings, scope and the source of collective responsibility, never in two paragraphs of prose.

keyPoints: The President is elected by elected MPs and elected MLAs, including those of Delhi and Puducherry, by single transferable vote.
Nominated members of Parliament and nominated MLAs do not vote in the Presidential election.
The President may be removed only for violation of the Constitution, by two thirds of each House in turn after fourteen days’ notice.
Executive action is taken in the President’s name, but the Council of Ministers advises on it under Article 74.
Legislative powers include summoning, proroguing and dissolving Parliament and promulgating ordinances under Article 123.
Judicial powers include pardon, reprieve, respite and remission, and an advisory reference to the Supreme Court under Article 143.
The Vice-President is elected by both Houses including nominated members and is removed only by a special resolution procedure.
The Vice-President is ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha and is not a member of that House.
The Prime Minister is appointed as the leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha; ministers are appointed on the Prime Minister’s advice.
The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha under Article 75(3) and individually responsible for its portfolios.
The Cabinet is the inner body that decides policy; its decisions bind the whole Council.
A minister who is not a member of either House must become one within six months.
examFocus: The Electoral College question is a trap question: mention elected members only, and name Delhi and Puducherry for the full mark.
On impeachment, quote the two-thirds of total membership requirement for each House and the fourteen days’ notice.
Any powers question must be organised under executive, legislative, financial, judicial, discretionary and emergency headings.
Council against Cabinet is a recurring distinguish pair: answer it in a table of size, meetings, scope and responsibility.

vocabulary.meaning: Elected MPs and elected MLAs who vote in the Presidential election.
Removal of the President for violation of the Constitution by the prescribed two-stage parliamentary procedure.
Law promulgated by the President under Article 123 when Parliament is not in session.
The complete or conditional remission of a sentence, a power vested in the President under Article 72.
The constitutional rule that the President acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers.
The rule that the whole Council answers for the government’s standing in the Lok Sabha.
A Minister of State attached to a Cabinet Minister, assisting without independent charge of the portfolio.
Ministers hold office during the President’s pleasure, exercisable only through the Prime Minister.

questions.prompt: The President of India is elected by:
options: Elected members of Parliament and elected members of State Assemblies
Both Houses of Parliament including nominated members
questions.answer: Elected members of Parliament and elected members of State Assemblies
questions.explanation: Article 54 limits the Electoral College to elected MPs and elected MLAs, including those of Delhi and Puducherry.

questions.prompt: Impeachment of the President requires a majority of:
options: Two thirds of the members present and voting
Two thirds of the total membership of each House
Two thirds of the Electoral College
questions.answer: Two thirds of the total membership of each House
questions.explanation: Each House must act by not less than two thirds of its total membership, first to make the charge and then to convict.

options: Elected members of both Houses only
All members of both Houses, nominated members included
questions.answer: All members of both Houses, nominated members included
questions.explanation: Unlike the Presidential election, the Vice-President’s election includes nominated members of both Houses.

questions.prompt: The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to:
questions.explanation: Article 75(3) makes the Council responsible to the Lok Sabha alone, which is why only the Lok Sabha can pass a no-confidence motion.

questions.prompt: The __________ of Ministers is appointed by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister.
questions.explanation: The whole body of ministers is appointed on the Prime Minister’s advice under Article 75(1).

questions.prompt: A person appointed a minister who is not a member of either House must become a member within __________ months.
questions.explanation: Article 75(5) gives six months, after which the ministership lapses.

questions.prompt: State two ways in which the election of the Vice-President differs from the election of the President.
questions.answer: First, nominated members of both Houses vote in the Vice-President’s election, whereas nominated members are excluded from the Presidential Electoral College. Second, the Vice-President is elected by Parliament alone, while the President is elected by Parliament together with the elected members of the State and certain Union Territory Assemblies.
questions.explanation: The inclusion of nominated members and the electorate being Parliament alone are the two differences that carry the marks.

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by the collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers.
questions.answer: Article 75(3) provides that the Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha, which means that the ministers act as a body and must retain the confidence of the Lok Sabha. If a no-confidence motion is passed, every minister must resign, and if any minister publicly disagrees with a policy the whole Council stands answerable for it. It also means that ministers must support one another in public and defend the government’s decisions in Parliament.
questions.explanation: Standing or falling together with the confidence of the Lok Sabha is the substance of the provision.

questions.prompt: Give two powers of the President that may be exercised without the advice of the Council of Ministers.
questions.answer: The President has two genuine discretionary areas: choosing the Prime Minister when no party or coalition commands a clear majority in the Lok Sabha, and selecting the leader to be appointed in that situation. In addition the President may require the Council to reconsider advice and may return it once, although the advice as reconsidered must be accepted.
questions.explanation: The choice of Prime Minister in a hung House is the true discretion; everything else runs on advice.

questions.prompt: Describe the procedure for the election of the President of India and state three qualifications and two grounds on which the President may be removed.
questions.answer: The President is elected by an Electoral College consisting of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States and of the legislatures of Delhi and Puducherry. The election is held by proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote and by secret ballot, and the value of each vote is adjusted so that the total value of the MPs’ votes and the total value of the MLAs’ votes are roughly equal. Nominated members do not vote. To stand, a candidate must be a citizen of India, at least 35 years of age and qualified to be elected a member of the Lok Sabha. The President may be removed only for violation of the Constitution: one House passes the charge by a majority of not less than two thirds of its total membership after fourteen days’ notice, the other House investigates and, if it agrees by the same majority, the President is removed from the date on which the resolution is passed.
questions.explanation: Electorate, system of voting, three qualifications and the two-stage two-thirds impeachment procedure all have to be present.

questions.prompt: Explain the powers of the President under the executive, legislative and financial heads, giving two instances of each.
questions.answer: Executive power: all executive action of the Union is taken in the President’s name, and the President appoints the Prime Minister, the other ministers on the Prime Minister’s advice, the Governors, the judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, the Attorney-General, the Comptroller and Auditor-General and the members of the Election Commission. Legislative power: the President summons and prorogues Parliament, dissolves the Lok Sabha, addresses the first session after a general election, and promulgates an ordinance under Article 123 when Parliament is not in session; no Bill becomes law without the President’s assent. Financial power: the annual financial statement showing the estimated receipts and expenditure of the Union is laid before Parliament in the President’s name, no bill involving expenditure from the Consolidated Fund may be introduced except on the President’s recommendation, and the Contingency Fund is at the President’s disposal during a recess.
questions.explanation: Each head needs two concrete instances with the recommendation and assent rules attached to the financial head.

questions.prompt: A minister publicly disagrees with the Cabinet on a policy and refuses to withdraw the statement. Analyse the constitutional position of the minister and the government in this situation.
questions.answer: The minister is in breach of two separate duties. Individually, each minister is answerable for the conduct of the portfolio and for the government’s policy line; public dissent shows that the minister no longer supports the position the Council has taken, and the convention is resignation or dismissal. Collectively, Article 75(3) binds the Council of Ministers to the confidence of the Lok Sabha, so a divided Council risks a confidence challenge: the government’s majority can only be counted if the ministers act together, and a Prime Minister who cannot command the House must advise a resignation or a test of confidence. The President would act on the Prime Minister’s advice in either step, since the doctrine of pleasure operates through the Prime Minister and not independently of it. The practical resolution is therefore resignation of the dissenting minister, or, if the Cabinet insists on the policy, dismissal; the government itself falls only if Parliament withdraws confidence.
questions.explanation: Individual responsibility requires the minister to fall in line or go, while collective responsibility exposes the whole government only if Parliament withdraws confidence.
